chapter_theme: Seven songs at Kumbakonam (கும்பகோணம், Kudanthai): a yogic vision of the dancing Lord of eight qualities in the jewelled hall within, pleas against women and their union, for jnana teaching and the sight of the space of knowledge, and two songs on the body, one on its ageing and one on its filth, asking for Sivayoga and jnana.
structure_note: 863 is a song of inner vision with no confession; 864 to 867 are courtesan songs (866 a short one); 868 is an ageing song and 869 a song of the body's impurity.

863.reading: The poet asks for the grace to see, where the light of moon and sun strikes the central pillar and the sweet taste of nectar-milk flows, the Lord of eight qualities dancing on the moon-bright seat in the jewelled hall, to see and rejoice in the fragrant petal of the letters, bathe in the sea of nectar, and behold the thousand and eight worlds. The praise, in drum syllables, shows the vel scattering Sura's crown as the seven seas surge, and names Murugan whom the daughter of the cloud-hued Vishnu, the golden doll, worships with hand-cymbals and praises, the six-faced lord of Kumbakonam.
863.nuance: The plea is a yogic vision in the Tirumanthiram's terms: moon and sun (இந்து, கதிர்), the central pillar (நடுத்தூண்), likely the central channel, the nectar, and the dance in the inner hall (மணிச்சபை). எண்குணமுற்றோன் is the Kural's எண்குணத்தான். கந்த எழுத்து, the fragrant letter, may mean the mystic syllable on a lotus petal, but the line is hard to divide.

864.reading: The poet asks whether he must wander for the women whose breasts leap like the tusks of an elephant, whose hair is like a cloud-dark night and a peacock's plumes, whose speech is molten gold and whose fish eyes shoot arrows that shatter the mind. The praise tells of Vishnu: as Rama, with his brother and Sita, who was drawn off by the forest deer and imprisoned until he broke the demons' crowns and freed her; as Krishna, blowing the horn and dancing as he gathered the herds; and names Murugan who delights in the breasts of the parrot-like girl, six-faced lord of Kumbakonam.
864.nuance: The plea is a single question; most of the song is the description and the praise of Vishnu's two avatars. The lines on Rama and the deer are hard to divide.

865.reading: The poet tells how at a glimpse of a woman's scented breasts he swells with desire, sinks into deceptive union and melts as a rogue, and asks not to wander thus but for Murugan to come, teach him the one thing in the meaning of jnana and give his fair feet daily. The praise names the vel that shattered Meru so the gods might live, and Murugan who cut the heads of those who imprisoned the loving ascetics of the Lord of the five gates, sending them to the stake while vultures pecked, lord of Kumbakonam among fields where conches crawl.
865.nuance: The praise seems to tell of enemies who harmed devotees of Siva being impaled, which recalls the Jains of the Sambandar story, though here they are called அசுரோர்; அஞ்சுவாயில் பரன், the Lord of the five gates, may mean the Lord reached through the five senses or the five letters. The reading is tentative.

866.reading: A short song: the poet asks whether, instead of sinking into the foul skin of dancing women with cotton-soft feet, he will gain Murugan's golden love through colourful Tamil of fine words. The praise names Murugan son of the Sakti who lives at the side of the god who fought Kama of the five arrows, lover of Devayanai's breasts, lord of Kumbakonam.
866.nuance: பங்கமார் தொக்கு, the soiled skin, reduces the women to their surface; the remedy is செஞ்சொல் சேர் சித்ரத் தமிழ், the poet's own art.

867.reading: The poet describes women who stand in the street at evening combing their scented hair, breasts and ornaments swaying, so that those passing on the road stagger at the sight, and asks that instead of suffering in thirst and dark delusion he may rise at dawn, recite Murugan's names, calling him son of loving Uma, know the right times and gain the grace for his eyes to see the space of knowledge. The praise names Kumaresa who stood in anger before Sura's army and the lord of Kumbakonam with a consort on either side.
867.nuance: The evening street and the morning worship are set against each other: மாலைதனில் ... காலையில் எழுந்து. ஞானவெளி கண்கள் காண, to see with the eyes the open space of knowledge, is the goal of the daily discipline.

868.reading: The poet pictures old age, black hair whitening, teeth falling, the mind clouded, dizziness and disease, the back bent, cough in the throat, the body shrunk and a stick shaking in the hand, the wife reviling him and the sons abusing him until he is a corpse, and asks when, the sea of birth of this filthy suffering body ended, he will reach the holy feet. The praise names the hero of the peacock-steed who churned the great sea, the vel that crushed the demons, Murugan proud on the breasts of the Kurava girl of the millet field, rider of the peacock, Kandha of Kudanthai.
868.nuance: The ageing is told through the household's scorn as much as the body: மனைவியும் நிந்தித்து அடுத்த மைந்தரும் வசைகள் விளம்ப. The praise line on the peacock as a steed (விரக துரங்கம்) is tentative.

869.reading: The poet speaks of the body born of water and phlegm, guts, flesh, rheum and cough, over which castes and disputants clamour about lineage, which all say is a disease of birth, of which they cry 'this is the Kali age' and 'take it to the burning ground', and which falls to dust, and asks that, instead of cherishing it with earrings, ornaments, clothes, arts and many desires, he be given the Sivayoga and jnana that remove them. The praise, in drum syllables, shows the vel against the Danava army, names Murugan who graces the great ascetics who know equanimity, who took refuge at the feet of the peacock-like girl in the millet field, the child who came through the tapas of Siva's bright flame, at Kudanthai.
869.nuance: பல சாதியும் வாதியும் இரைத்திடும் குலமே may say that the castes and sects quarrel over a body that is only filth, a rare social note, but the line is hard to read. சமத்து உணர்ந்திடு மாதவர், ascetics who know equanimity, are the model held up.

links.note: The Kural names God only as the one of eight qualities, whose feet the head must bow to; 863 takes the same epithet, எண்குணமுற்றோன், and places that Lord dancing in a hall within, to be seen in yogic vision.

Both picture old age with failing speech, lost teeth and a staff; the Naladiyar faults the old man who still stays in the house eyeing desire, while 868 adds the household's scorn and asks for the feet that end birth.
